To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the most important issue for service availability in a distributed system is the availability of the data service to the clients; 2) the most cost-effective way to achieve this is by using commodity hardware and software components; and 3) the most costeffective way to achieve HA data services for client-server computing is to use the HA Data Facility approach, which we illustrate in this paper.

1) the most important factor in achieving HA client-server computing is to design for the availability of data, not of machines, 2) HA data service is achieved by using dual-hosted disks and a software-based data replication protocol, 3) HA service can be achieved using commodity UNIX hardware (e.g., Sun SPARCstation 2's), and 4) HA service can also be achieved using commodity PC-based hardware, with the use of a PC-based disk replication protocol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
providing HA service to a large, distributed client network from a set of commodity UNIX machines.
the design of a general, cost-effective approach to HA data services for UNIX-based client-server networks.
a new approach to HA computing, based on commodity hardware and software components, and on the use of client-server networks to achieve the desired HA service.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HA is a system design goal, and that HA can be achieved with commodity UNIX hardware and commodity software components.

HA client-server data access is achievable using commodity hardware and software components; that it does not require complex, proprietary, and costly hardware; and that a “fault-tolerance”, or “fail-safe” approach is unnecessary.
fault-tolerant hardware is not the answer to the problem of highly-available data services.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HA data service can be achieved by combining a commodity UNIX operating system, a commodity UNIX network, and commodity UNIX hardware.

HA data access can be achieved at a reasonable cost, with commodity hardware and software, using a dual-hosted disk configuration, and a software architecture that supports the use of standard, off-the-shelf components.
HA data services can be provided with commodity hardware and software components, using standard protocols.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HA is achievable without fault-tolerant hardware, and that the key to HA is the availability of data services to the clients, rather than availability of a single server machine.
HA data service can be implemented using commodity components and that it is not necessary to depend on proprietary hardware or software to achieve HA.
HA data service for client-server networks can be provided using commodity components, and that the cost/performance of the solution is competitive with the cost/performance for non-HA systems.
